articleSummary: Measles with pneumonia claimed the life of a 26-year-old medical intern, AMW, at RSUD Cimacan in Cianjur, West Java, Indonesia, on 26 March 2026. The Indonesian Health Ministry expressed condolences and said the patient developed fever, red rash, and severe dyspnea before death despite medical management. The diagnosis is provisional: measles with pneumonia complications. Authorities from the Cianjur Health Office, West Java Health Office, and the Ministry of Health will conduct an Epidemiological Investigation (PE) to trace close contacts, identify the transmission source, and assess risk to curb further spread. The investigation aims to determine infection sources and prevent outbreaks, with ongoing surveillance and potential public health measures as needed. The report was released on 28 March 2026.

articleSummary: Measles, caused by Morbillivirus in the vaccine-preventable PD3I group, is highly contagious in Indonesia. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and can spread through airborne routes; the virus can survive on surfaces for hours, enabling infection from close contact or touching contaminated objects and then the nose or mouth. In crowded settings such as homes and schools, transmission accelerates, particularly among those without immunity. Measles is not limited to a rash; symptoms develop progressively and can lead to serious complications that drive mortality in some cases. High-risk groups include infants, unvaccinated children, and individuals with vitamin A deficiency; adolescents and young adults without complete immunization remain susceptible. The article does not report specific case counts or ongoing outbreaks.

Officials emphasize that measles can affect adults, and vaccination gaps can lead to severe outcomes; the recent rise in Cianjur is not limited to children.

articleHeadline: What Is Cyclospora Cayetanensis? The Gut Infection Behind Saba Azad's Hospitalisation, 4 Kg Weight Loss
articleSummary: Saba Azad was hospitalised after contracting Cyclospora cayetanensis, a gut infection causing her to lose about 4 kg over two weeks and suffer severe weakness. The illness commonly presents with watery or explosive diarrhoea, fatigue, bloating, nausea, vomiting, cramps, and can be serious enough to require hospital care. Cyclospora cayetanensis is transmitted through contaminated water and food, thriving in environmental temperatures around 22–32°C, and is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes infection occurs via contaminated produce or water, and is not directly communicable between people. Azad warned on food safety and shared a home-washed vegetables approach, mentioning baking soda as a washing method. Emphasized risks include the potential for prolonged symptoms in vulnerable individuals and the importance of thorough washing of leafy greens and vegetables to prevent infection.

articleSummary: HFMD is rising in Vietnam. In the first three months of 2025, about 25,094 HFMD cases were reported, five times higher than the same period in 2024 (4,900), with four deaths mainly in Ho Chi Minh City. The southern region accounts for about 72% of cases (18,031). The disease mainly affects children under 10 (99.3%), especially ages 1–5 in daycare. Authorities warn of Enterovirus 71 (EV71), a virulent strain that spreads rapidly and can cause severe complications and death, particularly in under-fives. Many cases lack the classic rash; lesions may appear in hidden areas like buttocks or around the anus, or only on finger/toe edges. Parents should check children during bathing, ensure adequate nutrition and hydration, and seek urgent care for fever over 39°C, dehydration, vomiting, or persistent cry/altered consciousness. Infected children should isolate for at least seven days; avoid puncturing blisters and self-medication with antibiotics.

Reinforce PHBS (Clean and Healthy Living) to prevent transmission and complete immunization status.

articleSummary: An emerging human ocular disease named POH-VAU is linked to aquatic-virus zoonosis. A Nature Microbiology study published on 26 March 2026 confirms CMNV (Covert Mortality Nodavirus), circulating in farmed and wild aquatic animals worldwide, is detected in the ocular tissue of 70 POH-VAU patients. Epidemiology indicates non-protected processing of aquatic animals and consumption of raw seafood account for 71.4% of confirmed cases. The findings provide the first direct link between an aquatic virus and a human eye disease, highlighting cross-species transmission. Virologist Dr. Anant Jongkaewwatta notes that animal-to-human transmission attention has typically focused on terrestrial wildlife; this study underscores aquatic-virus zoonoses as a source of new human disease. Public-health implications include precautions during seafood handling and consumption of raw aquatic products.

articleSummary: Meningococcal disease, caused by Neisseria meningitidis, can progress to meningitis or septic shock. In Thailand, emphasis is on prevention and vaccination. Meningitis may arise from multiple pathogens, but vaccines exist for bacteria with licensed protection: ACWY (A, C, W, Y) and MenB (B). ACWY is given from age 1+ in a single dose; it is recommended for travelers to Saudi Arabia (Hajj/Umrah) or Africa. MenB starts at 2 months. Serogroup B circulates overseas and outbreaks occur overseas, though it is less common in Thailand. Transmission is via close contact and respiratory droplets; incubation is about 2–10 days. Symptoms include fever, purpuric rash, neck/back stiffness, opisthotonus, photophobia, and rapid deterioration to shock. Treatments include immediate IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and steroids; close contacts receive chemoprophylaxis. Vaccination reduces severity and mortality; schedules vary by age and travel risk. Hospitals emphasize quality care and accredited standards; consultations are available at Navavej Hospital.

articleSummary: Cyclospora cayetanensis causes cyclosporiasis, an intestinal infection that targets the small intestine. In the case highlighted, actress Saba Azad endured two weeks of severe illness, losing 4 kg and requiring hospitalisation. The infection is not directly contagious between people, but it persists in the environment and is acquired by consuming food or water contaminated with feces. It thrives in 22-32°C climates and is a known risk with fresh produce irrigated or washed with contaminated water, including berries, basil, and lettuce, common in India. Symptoms include watery, explosive diarrhea; extreme fatigue; loss of appetite and rapid weight loss; stomach cramps, bloating, nausea, and low-grade fever. Prevention focuses on thorough washing of produce, including baking-soda soaks and vigorous friction to dislodge parasites; avoid relying on minimally washed triple-washed labels.

articleSummary: An international team led by Eliza Cabesa of the Universidad de la República in Uruguay reports Sporothrix brasiliensis, a fungus transmitted from cats to humans. Infections can cause deep skin ulcers often mistaken for bacterial infections, leading to unnecessary antibiotics. Infected cats harbor the fungus around the nose, mouth and paws, and fungal cells can be shed in droplets when they sneeze; scratches or bites provide entry to humans. The organism is dimorphic, existing as environmental hyphae that convert to yeast in warm human tissue, aiding skin colonization and persistence. High-risk groups include children under two, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Rarely, the fungus can involve the lungs, joints or meninges. The disease is curable with specific antifungal therapies, typically administered for about one month.

articleHeadline: Anthrax-causing bacteria have dwelled in soil for centuries - cycling through people, animals and earth
articleSummary: Anthrax-causing Bacillus anthracis persists in soil, forming communities around plant roots and cycling between land, livestock, and humans. In animals, spores ingested or entering via wounds germinate after macrophage uptake; bacteria produce toxins, causing rapid death in cattle within 48 hours, with spores returning to soil to persist for decades. Humans mostly contract through occupational exposure to animals (tanners, wool sorters, butchers). Spores survive 50+ years and resist dehydration, radiation, and chemicals. Historically, anthrax appeared in early Egypt and is described in Chinese texts; French explorers introduced spores to American soil in the early 1700s. In the 1930s–40s, Japanese forces released spores in Chinese villages; on Sept 18, 2001, mailed spores killed five in the United States. Inhalation is most deadly, with ~95% mortality historically without timely care. Treatments include antibiotics and monoclonal antibodies; vaccines by Greenfield and Pasteur circa 1881, now recommended for high-risk groups.

articleSummary: In Jiaozuo City, Henan Province, a stray dog entered a home through an unfixed door and bit resident Ms. Xin, resulting in a Category III (severe) rabies exposure. The dog died 3–4 days after the bite, and laboratory tests confirmed rabies virus positivity. The property management says disinfection of the dog’s activity areas was conducted twice and that authorities are coordinating with police; the street office will bolster disinfection and rabies prevention education in the district while awaiting investigation results. Public guidance urges immediate wound cleansing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seeking medical care for any skin breach or mucosal contact. The article outlines exposure levels I–III and the 2-1-1 vaccination schedule: Day 0 — two doses (one per arm); Days 7 and 21 — one dose each. Even vaccinated dogs can carry rabies; rabies immunoglobulin is indicated for certain III exposures. Vaccines are inactivated and safe for pregnancy, children, and the elderly.
